conceptName: When a threshold aborts a run

items.stem: What does the garbage-collection / orphan percentage abort threshold protect against?

options.text: Deleting or orphaning too much of the destination because of a bad source feed
The run taking too long
Duplicate POCO classes
A full disk on the StarBridge server

items.explanation: The percentage thresholds halt a run that would delete/orphan more than the allowed share of the destination — the classic symptom of a broken feed returning too few rows.

misconceptions.b: It's about how much would be removed, not runtime.

items.stem: A run aborts with a garbage-collection percentage error. What's the first thing to check?

options.text: Raise the threshold and re-run
How many source rows the feed loaded (a suspiciously low count = a broken feed)
Restart the StarBridge SQL server
Delete the orphaned mappings manually

items.explanation: Check the source row count first ('Loading source system entities ... N loaded'); a broken feed returning too few rows is the usual trigger.

misconceptions.a: Raising the threshold first can turn a caught problem into data loss.

items.stem: When is it appropriate to raise an abort threshold so the run completes?

options.text: Whenever an abort is slowing you down
Only once you've confirmed the large change is legitimate and expected (e.g. a real bulk removal)
Never — thresholds can't be changed
Any time the source feed looks fine at a glance

items.explanation: Raise it deliberately only when the big change is genuinely expected; otherwise the abort is correctly protecting the destination.

misconceptions.a: Forcing the run through to save time is exactly how a bad feed wipes the destination.

items.stem: An overnight run aborts: 'garbage-collection percentage exceeded.' The console shows the Staff feed loaded 120 entities; it normally loads ~5,000. What happened, and what do you do?
rubric: The source feed is broken/incomplete (120 vs ~5,000) — likely an outage, bad filter, or credential issue
The engine saw ~4,880 records as 'disappeared' and was about to garbage-collect them; the threshold aborted to protect the destination
Fix the source/feed and re-run; do NOT raise the threshold to force it through
items.sampleAnswer: The Staff feed only returned 120 of ~5,000, so it's broken (source outage, a bad query/filter, or a credential problem). The engine would have treated the ~4,880 missing records as deletions, and the GC threshold aborted to stop that — it did its job. I fix the source feed and re-run; I do not raise the threshold to push it through.
items.source: Documentation/Synnduit Deletion limit threshold setting demo.docx

items.stem: Which threshold is about 'too many errors' rather than 'too much deletion'?

options.text: SegmentAbortThreshold / RunAbortThreshold (exception counts)
GarbageCollectionPercentageAbortThreshold
OrphanMappingPercentageAbortThreshold
There is no error-count threshold

items.explanation: Segment/Run abort thresholds count exceptions; the percentage thresholds bound how much of the destination can be deleted/orphaned.

misconceptions.b: The GC percentage threshold bounds deletion, not error count.

items.stem: An orphan-mapping abort halted a run because a feed glitch returned too few rows. After you fix the feed, what is the correct recovery?

options.text: Just re-run — no StarBridge restore is needed, because the abort fires before any orphan mapping is deactivated or removed
Restore the StarBridge database from backup, then re-run
Manually delete the orphaned destination records first, then re-run
Lower the orphan threshold so the run completes, then re-run

items.explanation: The orphan-mapping check aborts before the step that changes any mapping state, so the mappings and destination records are untouched. Fix the feed and re-run — there's nothing to restore.

misconceptions.b: There's nothing to undo — the abort is preemptive, so the StarBridge state is intact.
misconceptions.c: The destination records were never removed; deleting them by hand would cause the very data loss the threshold prevented.
misconceptions.d: Forcing the run to complete would let the bad-feed removal proceed — the opposite of recovering.

items.source: lessons/L3.4.md - recovering after an orphan-mapping abort

items.stem: After the feed is fixed you re-run, and the earlier orphan-mapping abort had left the mappings intact. What outcome do the previously-missing records get?

options.text: NoChangesDetected — they match their existing mappings (or ChangesDetectedAndMerged if a value actually changed while the feed was down)
NewEntityCreated — they are treated as brand-new inserts
DuplicateDetectedNoChangesMerged — dedup re-matches them by [DuplicationKey]
ExceptionThrown — the mappings are now invalid

items.explanation: Because the mappings were never removed, the records match directly through the mapping lookup → NoChangesDetected. Dedup only runs for unmapped records, so duplicate detection isn't involved.

misconceptions.b: They're still mapped, so they aren't new inserts.
misconceptions.c: That path only happens if the mappings had actually been removed; here they're intact, so the records never reach dedup.

items.source: lessons/L3.4.md - recovering after an orphan-mapping abort

items.stem: Production abort thresholds are 5%. A small JSON feed of 10 records legitimately drops 1 (10%), so its runs keep aborting. What's the right response?

options.text: Raise the threshold for that specific migrator/segment — on a tiny dataset one record is already a large percentage, while large entities stay protected at 5%
Lower the global threshold so small feeds stop aborting
Remove the abort threshold entirely for all migrators
Restore StarBridge from backup and re-run at 5%

items.explanation: The threshold can be overridden per segment/migrator (a per-segment value takes precedence over the application default). Size it to what a legitimate run could plausibly remove: 5% suits a large entity (5% of 850,000 is a big loss), but false-trips a 10-record feed where one record is 10% — so raise it just for that migrator.

misconceptions.b: Lowering the threshold makes it more sensitive, not less — and changing the global value weakens protection for the large entities.
misconceptions.c: Removing the guard everywhere exposes large entities to the mass-deletion it exists to prevent.
misconceptions.d: Nothing needs restoring — this is a tuning question, not a recovery one.
